L101: If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 2 (Windows)](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-2-windows-install-the-aws-cli).
L102: ### Step 3: Log in to AWS
L103: 
L104: Configure the Region (gathered in "Before you start"), then sign in:
L105: 
L106: ```bash
L107: aws configure set region <region from prompt> --profile <profile_name>
L108: ```
L109: 
L110: ```bash
L111: aws login --region <region from prompt> --profile <profile_name>
L112: ```
L113: 
L114: A browser window will open for authentication. The human user will authenticate. If the human user wants to cancel this command at any time, let them. Wait for the command to exit before proceeding to Step 4.
L115: **Success:** `aws login` exits with code 0.
L116: 
L117: If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 3](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-3-log-in-to-aws).
L118: ### Step 4: Verify access
L119: 
L120: Verify AWS CLI access:
L121: 
L122: ```bash
L123: aws sts get-caller-identity --profile <profile_name>
L124: ```
L125: 
L126: **Success:** Returns AccountId, Arn, and UserId. Confirm to the user that credentials are working.
L127: 
L128: If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 4](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-4-verify-access).
L129: ### Step 5: Set up the Agent Toolkit
L130: 
L131: Run the following command to install AI coding agents, install default AWS skills, and configure the AWS MCP Server connection. This is an interactive wizard; let the human user complete any prompts.
L132: 
L133: ```bash
L134: aws configure agent-toolkit --yes --region us-east-1 --profile <profile_name>
L135: ```
L136: **Note:** The Agent Toolkit service is currently only available in `us-east-1`, regardless of your Region. Use `us-east-1` here and in Step 6 — do not substitute the user's current Region.
L137: 
L138: **Success:** Command exits with code 0.
L139: 
L140: If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 5](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-5-set-up-the-agent-toolkit).
L141: #### Point the AWS MCP Server at the user's profile
L142: The command above writes an `aws-mcp` server entry into each detected AI tool's MCP configuration file. That generated entry falls back to the `default` profile. Because this set up file always authenticates under a named `<profile_name>`, you MUST add that profile to each generated `aws-mcp` entry, or the MCP server will fail to start with `JSON-RPC error: -32602: Invalid request parameters("")` (it cannot locate credentials under the `default` profile).
L143: For each MCP configuration file the Agent Toolkit updated, open the file, locate the `aws-mcp` entry under `mcpServers`, and add (or merge in) an `env` block that sets `AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES` to `<profile_name>`. You MUST NOT remove or modify any other server entries, and you MUST leave the generated `command`, `args`, `timeout`, and `transport` values exactly as written — only add the `env` block:
L144: 
L145: ```json
L146: "env": {
L147:   "AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES": "<profile_name>"
L148: }
L149: ```
L150: 
L151: Notes:
L152: - Use `AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES` (not `AWS_PROFILE`) because it also enables cross-account switching later.
L153: - If you find an existing `aws-mcp` entry, ask the user how they want to reconcile the new changes.
L154: - If the MCP configuration file uses OpenCode, follow the OpenCode schema to modify the profile.
L155: - The Agent Toolkit determines each tool's MCP configuration file location automatically. If you need to locate or confirm a file, see the [Agent Toolkit documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/).
L156: After adding the `env` block, tell the user: "To use another AWS account later, run `aws login --profile <name>`, add that profile name to the space-separated `AWS_MCP_PROXY_PROFILES` list in each MCP configuration file, and restart your AI tool."
L157: ### Step 6: Verify Agent Toolkit installation
L158: 
L159: Run the following command to list all available skills in the remote catalog:
L160: 
L161: ```bash
L162: aws agent-toolkit list-available-skills --region us-east-1 --profile <profile_name>
L163: ```
L164: 
L165: **Success:** Returns a JSON of skills with name, description, skillVersion, and categories values.
L166: 
L167: If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 6](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-6-verify-agent-toolkit-installation).
L168: ### Step 7: Get AWS experience rule
L169: 
L170: Identify which AI coding tool is in use and its rules file location (this is not an exhaustive list):
L171: | Agent       | Project rules        | Location                  |
L172: | ----------- | -------------------- | ------------------------- |
L173: | Claude Code | CLAUDE.md            | Project root              |
L174: | Codex       | AGENTS.md            | Project root              |
L175: | Cursor      | .cursor/rules/\*.mdc | .cursor/rules/ directory  |
L176: | Kiro        | .kiro/steering/\*.md | .kiro/steering/ directory |
L177: | fx          | AGENTS.md            | Project root              |
L178: Retrieve the AWS experience rules file based on the AWS experience parameter and read its full contents:
L179: 
L180: - New AWS experience: <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws/refs/heads/main/rules/aws-starter-rules.md>
L181: - Advanced AWS experience: <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws/refs/heads/main/rules/aws-agent-rules.md>
L182: Then add the rules to each detected tool's rules file **without destroying existing content**. `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and files under `.cursor/rules/` or `.kiro/steering/` are the project's own agent instructions — often committed to version control and carrying accumulated project rules. You MUST NOT overwrite them.
L183: - If the rules file does **not** exist, create it (creating the directory if needed) and write the retrieved rules.
L184: - If the rules file **already exists**, append the retrieved rules under a clearly delimited heading rather than replacing the file. Use a stable marker so the operation is idempotent — for example, wrap the content between `<!-- BEGIN AWS Agent Toolkit rules -->` and `<!-- END AWS Agent Toolkit rules -->`. If that marked block is already present, replace only the content between the markers instead of appending a second copy.
L185: - If you cannot determine whether appending is safe (for example, an unfamiliar rules format), ask the user how they want to proceed before writing.
L186: Where a project's own instructions conflict with the AWS rules, the project's instructions take precedence.
L187: 
L188: **Success:** The AWS rules are present in the correct location for each AI tool, and any pre-existing project instructions are preserved. End the set up by telling the user:
L189: > Setup is complete! Close this session and start a new one. Your AI tool will automatically use the rules and skill files we just installed. Try this as your first prompt:
L190: >
L191: > Please make a single page webapp game and deploy it to AWS.
L192: >
L193: > If you're looking to explore what you can do on AWS, that prompt will get you started with a fun project. You can replace the game request with anything you'd like to build.
L194: If this step fails, see [Troubleshooting: Step 7](setup-troubleshooting.md#step-7-get-aws-experience-rule).

Setup stopped at AWS login. The `uv` install succeeded, and the connectivity check to AWS returned HTTP 200. I set the `Quickhealth` profile’s Region to `us-east-1`, but `aws login` exited with code 255 and reported:

aws: [ERROR]: [WinError 183] Cannot create a file when that file already exists: 'C:\\Users\\HP/.aws'

The setup’s troubleshooting guide doesn’t list this error and says to stop on unlisted failures, so I did not continue to credential verification or Agent Toolkit installation. # Developing with Streamlit

Streamlit (>=1.57) ships detailed reference documentation for building Streamlit apps inside its pip package. The bundled skill is a routing `SKILL.md` plus a `references/` folder of topic-specific reference docs (dashboards, themes, layouts, session state, custom components, etc.).

## Usage

Run the discovery script with the user's project directory:

```bash
python <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/discover.py --project-dir <USER_PROJECT_DIR>
```

The script prints either:

- **A path on stdout** (exit 0) â€” the bundled `SKILL.md`. Read it; it points into `references/`.
- **An `ERROR:` block on stderr** (non-zero exit). Follow the printed instructions and re-run.

`<SKILL_DIR>` is the directory containing this file; `<USER_PROJECT_DIR>` is the absolute path to the user's project. Passing `--project-dir` matters because the script resolves `.venv`, `../.venv`, `Pipfile`, `poetry.lock`, `pdm.lock`, and `uv.lock` relative to it.
# QuickHealth project instructions

## Project and working context
- QuickHealth is a 3-day neatHack project: an AI clerking assistant for nurses and health workers in Nigeria.
- It supports hospital-style history taking, including special pathways for children under 5 (including infants) and pregnant or postpartum women.
- This is a triage and history-taking tool, not a diagnostic tool.
- The project folder is `C:\Users\HP\Documents\quickhealth`. Work only inside this folder.
- The owner is new to coding. Explain steps in plain language and provide exact Windows PowerShell commands whenever they need to run something.
- The repository is already a Git repo, pushed to a public GitHub repository, with Entire CLI enabled to record sessions.

## Stack
- Python
- Streamlit interface
- SQLite for saved sessions
- OpenAI API; read `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_MODEL` from `.env`

## Hackathon requirements
- Use neatlogs tracing on every run. Install with `pip install "neatlogs[openai]"`.
- Read `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` from `.env` without printing, logging, committing, or asking the owner to paste any API key.
- Call `neatlogs.init(workflow_name="quickhealth-clerking", instrumentations=["openai"])` before importing `openai`.
- Wrap each clerking session in `@span(kind="WORKFLOW")` and call `neatlogs.flush()` so traces are sent.
- Give each architecture component its own traced span: intake and patient-type detection, adaptive clerking loop, rules-based red-flag checker, completeness verifier, contradiction checker, note generator, and SQLite state store.
- All code is written during the hackathon.
- Commit after every working step with a clear message and push to `origin main`, so Entire records checkpoints. Never rewrite Git history.

## Safety rules — always follow
- Never diagnose. Label any differential as **for clinician consideration**.
- Urgency (`EMERGENCY_NOW`, `SEE_CLINICIAN_TODAY`, `ROUTINE`) must be decided by a rules file, never by the language model. Escalate when unsure.
- Use only fictional patients. Never store or request real patient data.
- Show a clear notice in the app: this is not medical advice and users should call emergency services for danger signs.
- Never print, log, commit, or ask the owner to paste any API key. Keys belong only in `.env`, which must be in `.gitignore`.
- Never claim clinical validation.

## Working style
- Before big changes, present a plan and wait for the owner's approval.
- Make small changes and test after each one.
- Tell the owner exactly how to run and check the app.

# Developing with Streamlit

Streamlit (>=1.57) ships detailed reference documentation for building Streamlit apps inside its pip package. The bundled skill is a routing `SKILL.md` plus a `references/` folder of topic-specific reference docs (dashboards, themes, layouts, session state, custom components, etc.).

## Usage

Run the discovery script with the user's project directory:

```bash
python <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/discover.py --project-dir <USER_PROJECT_DIR>
```

The script prints either:

- **A path on stdout** (exit 0) â€” the bundled `SKILL.md`. Read it; it points into `references/`.
- **An `ERROR:` block on stderr** (non-zero exit). Follow the printed instructions and re-run.

`<SKILL_DIR>` is the directory containing this file; `<USER_PROJECT_DIR>` is the absolute path to the user's project. Passing `--project-dir` matters because the script resolves `.venv`, `../.venv`, `Pipfile`, `poetry.lock`, `pdm.lock`, and `uv.lock` relative to it.
# QuickHealth project instructions

## Project and working context
- QuickHealth is a 3-day neatHack project: an AI clerking assistant for nurses and health workers in Nigeria.
- It supports hospital-style history taking, including special pathways for children under 5 (including infants) and pregnant or postpartum women.
- This is a triage and history-taking tool, not a diagnostic tool.
- The project folder is `C:\Users\HP\Documents\quickhealth`. Work only inside this folder.
- The owner is new to coding. Explain steps in plain language and provide exact Windows PowerShell commands whenever they need to run something.
- The repository is already a Git repo, pushed to a public GitHub repository, with Entire CLI enabled to record sessions.

## Stack
- Python
- Streamlit interface
- SQLite for saved sessions
- OpenAI API; read `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_MODEL` from `.env`

## Hackathon requirements
- Use neatlogs tracing on every run. Install with `pip install "neatlogs[openai]"`.
- Read `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` from `.env` without printing, logging, committing, or asking the owner to paste any API key.
- Call `neatlogs.init(workflow_name="quickhealth-clerking", instrumentations=["openai"])` before importing `openai`.
- Wrap each clerking session in `@span(kind="WORKFLOW")` and call `neatlogs.flush()` so traces are sent.
- Give each architecture component its own traced span: intake and patient-type detection, adaptive clerking loop, rules-based red-flag checker, completeness verifier, contradiction checker, note generator, and SQLite state store.
- All code is written during the hackathon.
- Commit after every working step with a clear message and push to `origin main`, so Entire records checkpoints. Never rewrite Git history.

## Safety rules — always follow
- Never diagnose. Label any differential as **for clinician consideration**.
- Urgency (`EMERGENCY_NOW`, `SEE_CLINICIAN_TODAY`, `ROUTINE`) must be decided by a rules file, never by the language model. Escalate when unsure.
- Use only fictional patients. Never store or request real patient data.
- Show a clear notice in the app: this is not medical advice and users should call emergency services for danger signs.
- Never print, log, commit, or ask the owner to paste any API key. Keys belong only in `.env`, which must be in `.gitignore`.
- Never claim clinical validation.

## Working style
- Before big changes, present a plan and wait for the owner's approval.
- Make small changes and test after each one.
- Tell the owner exactly how to run and check the app.

"""SQLite persistence for fictional clerking sessions."""

import json
import sqlite3
import time
import uuid
from pathlib import Path
from contextlib import contextmanager

import neatlogs
from opentelemetry import trace as otel_trace

DB_PATH = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "data" / "quickhealth.sqlite3"


@contextmanager
def _connect():
    DB_PATH.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    connection = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    try:
        connection.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sessions (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, history TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]', note TEXT, summary TEXT, urgency TEXT, patient_type TEXT, created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)")
        columns = {row[1] for row in connection.execute("PRAGMA table_info(sessions)")}
        for name, definition in (
            ("input_tokens", "INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0"),
            ("output_tokens", "INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0"),
            ("model_latency_ms", "REAL NOT NULL DEFAULT 0"),
        ):
            if name not in columns:
                connection.execute(f"ALTER TABLE sessions ADD COLUMN {name} {definition}")
        connection.commit()
        yield connection
        connection.commit()
    except Exception:
        connection.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        connection.close()


@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", name="sqlite_write_recovery", capture_input=False, capture_output=False)
def _retry_sqlite_write(operation, write):
    """Retry only transient SQLite lock/busy errors; never expose database text to traces."""
    span = otel_trace.get_current_span()
    attempts = 0
    recovered = False
    status = "not_needed"
    try:
        for attempts in range(1, 4):
            try:
                value = write()
                recovered = attempts > 1
                status = "recovered" if recovered else "not_needed"
                return value
            except sqlite3.OperationalError as exc:
                message = str(exc).casefold()
                if "locked" not in message and "busy" not in message:
                    status = "failed"
                    raise
                if attempts == 3:
                    status = "failed"
                    raise
                if span and span.is_recording():
                    span.add_event("sqlite_write_retry", {"attempt": attempts, "error_category": "sqlite_busy"})
                time.sleep(0.05 * attempts)
        raise RuntimeError("SQLite retry loop ended unexpectedly")
    finally:
        if span and span.is_recording():
            span.set_attribute("quickhealth.storage.operation", operation)
            span.set_attribute("quickhealth.storage.attempt_count", attempts)
            span.set_attribute("quickhealth.storage.retry_count", max(0, attempts - 1))
            span.set_attribute("quickhealth.storage.recovered", recovered)
            span.set_attribute("quickhealth.storage.recovery_status", status)


def record_model_usage(session_id, input_tokens, output_tokens, latency_ms):
    """Persist only aggregate usage metrics; no prompts or response text are stored here."""
    with _connect() as connection:
        connection.execute(
            "UPDATE sessions SET input_tokens = input_tokens + ?, output_tokens = output_tokens + ?, "
            "model_latency_ms = model_latency_ms + ? WHERE id = ?",
            (max(0, int(input_tokens)), max(0, int(output_tokens)), max(0.0, float(latency_ms)), session_id),
        )


def completed_usage_totals():
    """Return token/time totals for completed sessions only."""
    with _connect() as connection:
        row = connection.execute(
            "SELECT COUNT(*), COALESCE(SUM(input_tokens),0), COALESCE(SUM(output_tokens),0), "
            "COALESCE(SUM(model_latency_ms),0) FROM sessions WHERE note IS NOT NULL "
            "AND (input_tokens > 0 OR output_tokens > 0)"
        ).fetchone()
    return {"sessions": row[0], "input_tokens": row[1], "output_tokens": row[2], "latency_ms": row[3]}


@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", name="sqlite_state_store_create", capture_input=False, capture_output=False)
def create_session():
    session_id = str(uuid.uuid4())[:8]
    def write():
        with _connect() as connection:
            connection.execute("INSERT INTO sessions (id) VALUES (?)", (session_id,))
    _retry_sqlite_write("create_session", write)
    return session_id


@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", name="sqlite_state_store_get", capture_input=False, capture_output=False)
def get_session(session_id):
    with _connect() as connection:
        row = connection.execute("SELECT id, history, note, summary, urgency, patient_type FROM sessions WHERE id = ?", (session_id,)).fetchone()
    return row


@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", name="sqlite_state_store_list", capture_input=False, capture_output=False)
def list_sessions():
    with _connect() as connection:
        return connection.execute("SELECT id FROM sessions ORDER BY created_at DESC").fetchall()


@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", name="sqlite_state_store_save_answer", capture_input=False, capture_output=False)
def save_answer(session_id, question, answer):
    def write():
        with _connect() as connection:
            row = connection.execute("SELECT history FROM sessions WHERE id = ?", (session_id,)).fetchone()
            history = json.loads(row[0]) if row else []
            history.extend([
                {"role": "assistant", "content": question},
                {"role": "user", "content": answer},
            ])
            connection.execute("UPDATE sessions SET history = ? WHERE id = ?", (json.dumps(history), session_id))
    _retry_sqlite_write("save_answer", write)


@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", name="sqlite_state_store_save_result", capture_input=False, capture_output=False)
def save_result(session_id, note, summary, urgency, patient_type):
    def write():
        with _connect() as connection:
            connection.execute(
                "UPDATE sessions SET note = ?, summary = ?, urgency = ?, patient_type = ? WHERE id = ?",
                (note, summary, urgency, patient_type, session_id),
            )
    _retry_sqlite_write("save_result", write)


@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", name="sqlite_state_store_verification_get", capture_input=False, capture_output=False)
def get_verification_state(session_id):
    with _connect() as connection:
        columns = {row[1] for row in connection.execute("PRAGMA table_info(sessions)")}
        if "verification_state" not in columns:
            connection.execute("ALTER TABLE sessions ADD COLUMN verification_state TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'")
        row = connection.execute("SELECT verification_state FROM sessions WHERE id = ?", (session_id,)).fetchone()
    try:
        value = json.loads(row[0]) if row and row[0] else {}
        return value if isinstance(value, dict) else {}
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError):
        return {}


@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", name="sqlite_state_store_verification_save", capture_input=False, capture_output=False)
def save_verification_state(session_id, state):
    with _connect() as connection:
        columns = {row[1] for row in connection.execute("PRAGMA table_info(sessions)")}
        if "verification_state" not in columns:
            connection.execute("ALTER TABLE sessions ADD COLUMN verification_state TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'")
        connection.execute(
            "UPDATE sessions SET verification_state = ? WHERE id = ?",
            (json.dumps(state, ensure_ascii=True), session_id),
        )

def configure_tracing():
    neatlogs.init(

        instrumentations=["openai"],
        mask=redact_trace_content,

    return True

from quickhealth.pathways import select_pathway
from quickhealth.storage import (
    create_session,
    get_session,
    get_verification_state,
    list_sessions,
)
from quickhealth.ui import apply_app_style, pending_conflict_count, render_pathway_card, render_progress
from quickhealth.verification import completeness_check
from quickhealth.workflow import process_answer


st.set_page_config(page_title="QuickHealth", page_icon=":material/health_and_safety:", layout="wide")
apply_app_style(st)
st.title("QuickHealth", icon=":material/health_and_safety:")
st.caption("A calm, structured clerking workspace for fictional cases")
with st.container(border=True):
    st.error(
        "Fictional cases only. Not medical advice. Call emergency services for danger signs. "
        "This tool does not diagnose.",
        icon=":material/emergency:",
    )
    st.info("Do not enter real patient names, contact details, or any real patient information.", icon=":material/lock:")


def model_client():
    """Create the OpenAI client only when the owner has configured a key."""
    if not CONFIG.get("OPENAI_API_KEY"):
        st.error("OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your local .env file, then restart Streamlit.")
        st.stop()
    if not CONFIG.get("OPENAI_MODEL"):
        st.error("OPENAI_MODEL is missing. Add it to your local .env file, then restart Streamlit.")
        st.stop()
    return OpenAI(api_key=CONFIG["OPENAI_API_KEY"])


sessions = list_sessions()
with st.sidebar:
    st.subheader("Fictional sessions", icon=":material/folder_open:")
    with st.container(border=True):
        fictional_confirmed = st.checkbox("I confirm this case is entirely fictional")
        if st.button("Start a new fictional case", type="primary", disabled=not fictional_confirmed, icon=":material/add:"):
            st.session_state.session_id = create_session()
            st.session_state.history = []
            st.session_state.next_question = "Describe a fictional patient using a made-up age and no identifying details. What is the main concern today?"
            st.session_state.result = None
            st.session_state.verification_state = {}
    if sessions:
        with st.container(border=True):
            st.caption(f"Saved fictional cases Â· {len(sessions)}")
            saved_ids = [row[0] for row in sessions]
            selected_id = st.selectbox("Choose a saved case", [""] + saved_ids)
            if selected_id and st.button("Open saved case", icon=":material/folder_open:"):
                row = get_session(selected_id)
                st.session_state.session_id = selected_id
                st.session_state.history = json.loads(row[1])
                st.session_state.verification_state = get_verification_state(selected_id)
                st.session_state.next_question = "Continue the fictional history with one question at a time."
                st.session_state.result = (
                    {"note": row[2], "summary": row[3], "urgency": row[4], "missing": [], "contradictions": []}
                    if row[2]
                    else None
                )

if "session_id" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.session_id = None
if st.session_state.session_id is None:
    st.write("Start a fictional case to begin. QuickHealth asks one question at a time and adapts follow-up questions to earlier answers.")
    st.stop()

session_id = st.session_state.session_id
history = st.session_state.get("history", [])
st.session_state.setdefault("verification_state", {})
patient_type = select_pathway(history) if history else "unknown"
current_completeness = completeness_check(
    patient_type,
    st.session_state.get("verification_state", {}).get("completeness", {}),
)
lmp_estimate = find_lmp_estimate(history) if patient_type.startswith("pregnancy_") else None
render_pathway_card(st, patient_type)
render_progress(st, current_completeness)
pending_conflicts = pending_conflict_count(st.session_state.get("verification_state", {}))
if pending_conflicts and not st.session_state.get("result"):
    st.warning(
        f"Possible inconsistency detected ({pending_conflicts}). Please answer the clarification question below before continuing.",
        icon=":material/warning:",
    )
if lmp_estimate and lmp_estimate["status"] == "estimated":
    st.info(
        f"LMP-based estimate only â€” EDD {lmp_estimate['edd']}; "
        f"gestational age {lmp_estimate['weeks']} weeks and {lmp_estimate['days']} days. "
        + LMP_ESTIMATE_NOTICE
    )
elif lmp_estimate and lmp_estimate["status"] in {"uncertain", "invalid", "future"}:
    st.warning("LMP date is uncertain, invalid, or in the future; no date estimate is shown. " + LMP_ESTIMATE_NOTICE)

if st.session_state.get("result"):
    result = st.session_state.result
    if result.get("emergency"):
        st.error("EMERGENCY â€” stop the questionnaire and seek emergency care now. Call emergency services or go to the nearest hospital.")
        st.write(result["message"])
        st.subheader("Urgency from safety rules")
        st.write(result["urgency"])
        st.stop()
    if result.get("incomplete") or result.get("blocked"):
        st.warning(result.get("message", "Required details remain unresolved; the session is not complete."))
        st.subheader("Urgency from safety rules")
        if result.get("urgency"):
            st.write(result["urgency"])
        if result.get("missing"):
            st.subheader("Still missing or unknown")
            st.write(", ".join(result["missing"]))
        if result.get("contradictions"):
            st.subheader("Possible conflicts still needing clarification")
            for pair in result["contradictions"]:
                st.write(" â€¢ ".join(pair))
        st.write("No final note was generated because verification is unresolved.")
        st.stop()
    st.subheader("Structured clerking note", icon=":material/clinical_notes:")
    with st.container(border=True):
        st.markdown(result["note"])
    st.subheader("Plain-language summary", icon=":material/subject:")
    with st.container(border=True):
        st.write(result["summary"])
    st.subheader("Urgency from safety rules")
    st.write(result["urgency"])
    if result["missing"]:
        st.caption("Sections that may need more information: " + ", ".join(result["missing"]))
    if result["contradictions"]:
        st.warning("Please clarify these possible inconsistencies: " + "; ".join(result["contradictions"]))
    if st.button("Start another fictional case"):
        st.session_state.session_id = create_session()
        st.session_state.history = []
        st.session_state.next_question = "Describe a fictional patient using a made-up age and no identifying details. What is the main concern today?"
        st.session_state.result = None
        st.session_state.verification_state = {}
        st.rerun()
else:
    if not history:
        st.session_state.next_question = "Describe a fictional patient using a made-up age and no identifying details. What is the main concern today?"
    for item in history:
        with st.chat_message(item["role"], avatar=":material/health_and_safety:" if item["role"] == "assistant" else None):
            st.write(item["content"])
    with st.chat_message("assistant", avatar=":material/health_and_safety:"):
        st.write(st.session_state.next_question)
    answer = st.chat_input("Answer for this fictional case", max_chars=4000)
    if answer:
        client = model_client()
        try:
            updated_history, next_question, result, verification_state = process_answer(
                client, session_id, history, answer, st.session_state.next_question,
                st.session_state.get("verification_state", {}),
            )
            st.session_state.history = updated_history
            st.session_state.verification_state = verification_state
            if result:
                st.session_state.result = result
            else:
                st.session_state.next_question = next_question
        except Exception:
            # Never display exception text because provider errors can contain request details.
            st.error("QuickHealth could not complete that step. Check your local setup and try again.")
        finally:
            neatlogs.flush()
        st.rerun()

# Developing with Streamlit

This is a **routing skill** that directs you to specialized references for Streamlit development.

## When to Use

Invoke this skill when the user's request involves:
- Creating a new Streamlit app
- Editing or modifying an existing Streamlit app
- Debugging Streamlit issues (errors, session state bugs, performance problems)
- Beautifying or improving the visual design of a Streamlit app
- Optimizing Streamlit performance (caching, fragments, reruns)
- Building and running Streamlit apps
- Building chat, conversational, or agentic UIs (AI assistants, thinking expanders, chain-of-thought, tool-call timelines)
- Styling widgets (button colors, backgrounds, CSS customization)
- Advanced server configuration with `st.App`, ASGI, Starlette, FastAPI integration, custom routes, middleware, or lifespan hooks
- Any question about Streamlit widgets, layouts, or components

**Trigger phrases:** "streamlit", "st.", "st.App", "dashboard", "app.py", "beautify app", "make it look better", "style", "CSS", "color", "background", "theme", "button", "slow rerun", "session state", "performance", "faster", "cache", "chat", "agentic", "chain of thought"

## Workflow

```
Step 1: Locate the Streamlit source code

Step 2: Identify task type and load appropriate reference(s)

Step 3: Apply guidance from reference to edit code

Step 4: Check if app is running and offer to run it
```

### Step 1: Locate the Streamlit Source Code (if needed)

**Goal:** Identify the app file(s) to edit. **Skip this step if already clear from context.**

**When to skip:**
- User mentioned a specific file path (e.g., "edit `src/app.py`")
- User has file(s) already in conversation context
- Working directory has an obvious single entry point (`app.py`, `streamlit_app.py`)

**When to search:**
- User says "my streamlit app" without specifying which file
- Multiple Python files exist and it's unclear which is the entry point

**If searching is needed:**

1. **Quick scan** for Streamlit files:
   ```bash
   grep -rl 'import streamlit\|from streamlit' --include='*.py' . 2>/dev/null | head -10
   ```

2. **Apply entry point heuristics** (in priority order):
   - `streamlit_app.py` at root â†’ **this is the entry point** (canonical name)
   - `app.py` at root â†’ likely entry point
   - File using `st.navigation` â†’ entry point for multi-page apps
   - Single `.py` file at root with streamlit import â†’ entry point
   - Files in `pages/` or `app_pages/` subdirectory â†’ **NOT entry points** (these are sub-pages)

3. **If entry point is obvious** â†’ use it, no confirmation needed

   Example: Found `streamlit_app.py` and `pages/metrics.py` â†’ use `streamlit_app.py`

4. **Only ask if genuinely ambiguous** (e.g., multiple root-level candidates, none named `streamlit_app.py`):
   ```
   Found multiple potential entry points:
   - dashboard.py
   - main.py

   Which is your main app?
   ```

**Output:** Path to the main Streamlit source file(s)

### Step 2: Identify Task Type and Route to Reference

**Goal:** Determine what the user needs and load the appropriate guidance.

**IMPORTANT â€” `use_container_width` is deprecated.** Never add `use_container_width` to new code. Streamlit elements now stretch to fill their container by default. Use `width="stretch"` or `width="content"` instead. Remove `use_container_width` when you encounter it.

### Proactively Look Up API Details

When selecting a Streamlit command, discovering functionality that may be newer than the agent's knowledge cutoff, validating available functionality, or using unfamiliar parameters, proactively look up the relevant local docs before coding:

```bash
streamlit docs st.<command>
```

Run this with the Streamlit installation relevant to the app being edited. Use `references/api-reference.md` to discover available public `st` commands and namespaces, then use `streamlit docs st.<command>` for exact signatures, parameters, and docstrings.

When annotating Streamlit-owned values returned by commands or stored in Session State, import the curated public types from `streamlit.typing` (also available as `st.typing`) instead of their internal implementation modules. See `references/api-reference.md` for the available types.

### Best practices quick reference

Apply these defaults unless the user's app or request clearly needs a different approach. For examples, read `references/best-practices.md`.
- Do not use `use_container_width`; use `width="stretch"` or `width="content"` instead.
- Prefer native Streamlit elements over recreating UI with custom HTML. This includes UI created with `st.html`, `st.markdown(..., unsafe_allow_html=True)`, or deprecated `st.components.v1.html`. Use custom HTML only when no native element provides the required UI or behavior.
- Do not use the deprecated `st.components.v1.html` or `st.components.v1.iframe` commands. Use `st.iframe` for iframe-based rendering of URLs or HTML, and use `st.html` for HTML/CSS that should render directly in the app; `st.html` ignores JavaScript by default unless `unsafe_allow_javascript=True`.
- Do not apply CSS to style the app unless the user actively requests it. Use native Streamlit features and `.streamlit/config.toml` to customize the appearance; see the [theming reference](references/theme.md).
- Prefer Material Symbols icons (`:material/icon_name:`) over emojis for navigation, buttons, and labels. Use emojis sparingly, only when they add a special touch.
- Prefer sentence casing over title casing, including titles and widget labels.
- Do not use empty widget labels; use `label_visibility="collapsed"` or `label_visibility="hidden"` when a visible label is not desired.
- Pass keyword-only `alt=` on images, charts, maps, media, iframes, PDFs, tables, dataframes, and data editors so assistive technologies can name them. Keep it short; decorative `alt=""` is only for `st.image` / `st.pyplot`. See `references/media-display.md` and `references/data-display.md`.
- Use `st.container(border=True)` for simple visual grouping. Prefer `st.container(horizontal=True)` over `st.columns` for responsive row layouts; use `st.columns` only for fixed grids or precise width ratios.
- Prefer `st.navigation` and `st.Page` with an `app_pages/` folder over the legacy `pages/` directory, `st.page_link`, or other multipage-app v1 patterns.
- Always cache compute-intensive or expensive data-loading code. Use `st.cache_data` for serializable data and `st.cache_resource` for shared resources like API clients, raw connectors, and models; do not wrap `st.connection`, which is already cached. Include appropriate `ttl` and/or `max_entries` limits to prevent unbounded growth. Cache the expensive source data, then apply cheap interactive filters outside the cached function.
- Order scripts so fast UI (titles, layout, widgets) renders before slow computation. Streamlit streams elements top to bottom and temporarily greys out (marks stale) not-yet-redrawn elements from the previous run while a slow step is in progress, clearing each as the new run recreates it; put slow work last, reserve output slots with `st.container()`, or isolate slow sections in fragments.
- Use `st.fragment` for independent sections that should rerun separately from the rest of the app, such as auto-refreshing charts or controls that do not need to rerun the full page.
- Use `st.form` to batch related inputs and rerun only on submit, especially when intermediate widget changes would trigger expensive work.
- Do not put expensive work unguarded inside `st.tabs` or `st.expander`; hidden or collapsed content still computes unless you use dynamic open-state gating or an explicit conditional.
- Use `st.secrets` for credentials. Never hard-code secrets in app code, never commit `.streamlit/secrets.toml`, and use parameterized queries for user-provided values.
- Prefer Vega-based charts (`st.altair_chart`, `st.line_chart`, `st.area_chart`, `st.scatter_chart`, `st.bar_chart`, `st.vega_lite_chart`) over `st.pyplot` and Plotly. Use `st.echarts_chart` when you already have an Apache ECharts option or a `pyecharts` chart.
- Prefer `st.segmented_control` over `st.radio(..., horizontal=True)`.
- Use `st.pills` for a multiselect with a small number of options that fit on one line.
- Initialize `st.session_state` in one clear place, avoid module-level mutable state for per-user data, and set widget `key` values when widgets repeat, parameters change dynamically, or code needs programmatic access.
- Keep page files as direct scripts; do not wrap page bodies in functions. Move shared business logic into modules.

A visitor could see another visitor’s fictional conversation. The app also reads API keys from `.env`, while Streamlit Cloud uses its own secrets settings.

## Task 2: Allow inbound traffic from the EC2 Instance Connect service to your instance

When you use EC2 Instance Connect in the Amazon EC2 console to connect to an instance, the traffic that must be allowed to reach the instance is traffic from the EC2 Instance Connect service. This is different to connecting from your local computer to an instance; in that case, you must allow traffic from your local computer to your instance. To allow traffic from the EC2 Instance Connect service, you must create a security group that allows inbound SSH traffic from the IP address range for the EC2 Instance Connect service.

AWS uses prefix lists to manage IP address ranges. The names of the EC2 Instance Connect prefix lists are as follows, with `region` replaced by the Region code:

  * IPv4 prefix list name: `com.amazonaws.`region`.ec2-instance-connect`

  * IPv6 prefix list name: `com.amazonaws.`region`.ipv6.ec2-instance-connect`

Task objective

You'll create a security group that allows inbound SSH traffic on port 22 from the IPv4 prefix list in the Region in which your instance is located.

###### To create a security group that allows inbound traffic from the EC2 Instance Connect service to your instance

  1. Open the Amazon EC2 console at https://console.aws.amazon.com/ec2/.

  2. In the navigation pane, choose Security Groups.

  3. Choose Create security group.

  4. Under Basic details, do the following:

    1. For Security group name, enter a meaningful name for your security group.

    2. For Description, enter a meaningful description for your security group.

  5. Under Inbound rules, do the following:

    1. Choose Add rule.

    2. For Type, choose SSH.

    3. For Source, leave Custom.

    4. In the field next to Source, select the prefix list for EC2 Instance Connect.

For example, if your instance is located in the US East (N. Virginia) (`us-east-1`) Region and your users will connect to its public IPv4 address, choose the following prefix list: com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ec2-instance-connect

  6. Choose Create security group.

## Task 3: Launch your instance

  1. Open the Amazon EC2 console at https://console.aws.amazon.com/ec2/.

  2. In the navigation bar at the top of the screen, the current AWS Region is displayed (for example, Ireland). Select a Region in which to launch your instance. This choice is important because you created a security group that allows traffic for a specific Region, so you must select the same Region in which to launch your instance.

  3. From the Amazon EC2 console dashboard, choose Launch instance.

  4. (Optional) Under Name and tags, for Name, enter a descriptive name for your instance.

  5. Under Application and OS Images (Amazon Machine Image), choose Quick Start. Amazon Linux is selected by default. Under Amazon Machine Image (AMI), Amazon Linux 2023 AMI is selected by default. Keep the default selection for this task.

  6. Under Instance type, for Instance type, keep the default selection, or choose a different instance type.

  7. Under Key pair (login), for Key pair name, choose Proceed without a key pair (Not recommended). When you use EC2 Instance Connect to connect to an instance, EC2 Instance Connect pushes a key pair to the instance's metadata, and it is this key pair that is used for the connection.

  8. Under Network settings, do the following:

    1. For Auto-assign public IP, leave Enable.

###### Note

To use EC2 Instance Connect in the Amazon EC2 console to connect to an instance, the instance must have a public IPv4 or IPv6 address.

    2. For Firewall (security groups), choose Select existing security group.

    3. Under Common security groups, choose the security group that you created earlier.

  9. In the Summary panel, choose Launch instance.

# stop-instances¶

## Description¶

Stops an Amazon EBS-backed instance. You can restart your instance at any time using the StartInstances API. For more information, see Stop and start Amazon EC2 instances in the Amazon EC2 User Guide .

When you stop or hibernate an instance, we shut it down. By default, this includes a graceful operating system (OS) shutdown. To bypass the graceful shutdown, use the `skipOsShutdown` parameter; however, this might risk data integrity.

You can use the StopInstances operation together with the `Hibernate` parameter to hibernate an instance if the instance is enabled for hibernation and meets the hibernation prerequisites . Stopping an instance doesn’t preserve data stored in RAM, while hibernation does. If hibernation fails, a normal shutdown occurs. For more information, see Hibernate your Amazon EC2 instance in the Amazon EC2 User Guide .

If your instance appears stuck in the `stopping` state, there might be an issue with the underlying host computer. You can use the StopInstances operation together with the Force parameter to force stop your instance. For more information, see Troubleshoot Amazon EC2 instance stop issues in the Amazon EC2 User Guide .

Stopping and hibernating an instance differs from rebooting or terminating it. For example, a stopped or hibernated instance retains its root volume and any data volumes, unlike terminated instances where these volumes are automatically deleted. For more information about the differences between stopping, hibernating, rebooting, and terminating instances, see Amazon EC2 instance state changes in the Amazon EC2 User Guide .

We don’t charge for instance usage or data transfer fees when an instance is stopped. However, the root volume and any data volumes remain and continue to persist your data, and you’re charged for volume usage. Every time you start your instance, Amazon EC2 charges a one-minute minimum for instance usage, followed by per-second billing.

You can’t stop or hibernate instance store-backed instances.

## Synopsis¶
    
      stop-instances
    --instance-ids <value>
    [--hibernate | --no-hibernate]
    [--skip-os-shutdown | --no-skip-os-shutdown]

# Detach an Amazon EBS volume from an Amazon EC2 instance

You need to detach an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume from an instance before you can attach it to a different instance or delete it. Detaching a volume does not affect the data on the volume.

## Considerations

  * You can detach an Amazon EBS volume from an instance explicitly or by terminating the instance. However, if the instance is running, you must first unmount the volume from the instance.

  * If an EBS volume is the root device of an instance, you must stop the instance before you can detach the volume.

  * You can reattach a volume that you detached (without unmounting it), but it might not get the same mount point. If there were writes to the volume in progress when it was detached, the data on the volume might be out of sync.

  * After you detach a volume, you are still charged for volume storage as long as the storage amount exceeds the limit of the AWS Free Tier. You must delete a volume to avoid incurring further charges. For more information, see Delete an Amazon EBS volume.

## Unmount and detach a volume

Use the following procedures to unmount and detach a volume from an instance. This can be useful when you need to attach the volume to a different instance or when you need to delete the volume.

###### Steps

  * Step 1: Unmount the volume

  * Step 2: Detach the volume from the instance

  * Step 3: (Windows instances only) Uninstall the offline device locations

### Step 1: Unmount the volume

From your Linux instance, use the following command to unmount the `/dev/sdh` device.
    
    ``[ec2-user ~]$ ``sudo umount -d `/dev/sdh```

From your Windows instance, unmount the volume as follows.

  1. Start the Disk Management utility.

     * (Windows Server 2012 and later) On the taskbar, choose (right-click) the Windows logo and choose Disk Management.

     * Windows Server 2008) Choose Start, Administrative Tools, Computer Management, Disk Management.

How instance termination works - Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud

ConsiderationsWhat happens when you terminate an instanceTest application response

When you terminate an instance, changes are registered at the operating system (OS) level of the instance, some resources are lost, and some resources persist.

The following diagram shows what is lost and what persists when an Amazon EC2 instance is terminated. When an instance terminates, the data on any instance store volumes and the data stored in the instance RAM is erased. Any Elastic IP addresses associated with the instance are detached. For Amazon EBS root volumes and data volumes, the outcome depends on the Delete on termination setting of each volume.

Image: The IP addresses, RAM, instance store volumes, and EBS root volume are lost when an instance is terminated.

## Considerations

  * Data persistence

    * Instance store volumes: All data is permanently deleted when the instance terminates.

    * EBS root volume:

      * When attached at launch, deleted by default when the instance terminates.

      * When attached after launch, persists by default when the instance terminates.

    * EBS data volumes:

      * When attached at launch using the console: Persists by default when the instance terminates.

      * When attached at launch using the CLI: Deleted by default when the instance terminates.

      * When attached after launch using the console or CLI: Persists by default when the instance terminates.

###### Note

Any volumes that are not deleted on instance termination continue to incur charges. You can change the setting so that a volume is deleted or persists on instance termination. For more information, see Preserve data when an instance is terminated.

  * Protection against accidental termination

    * To prevent an instance from being accidentally terminated by someone, enable termination protection.

# Preserve data when an instance is terminated

When an Amazon EC2 instance is terminated, you can preserve the data on your instance store volumes or Amazon EBS volumes. This topic explains how to ensure your data persists beyond instance termination.

## How instance termination affects root and data volumes

###### Instance store volumes

When an instance is terminated, the instance store volumes are automatically deleted and the data is lost. To preserve this data beyond the lifetime of the instance, before terminating the instance, manually copy the data to persistent storage, such as an Amazon EBS volume, an Amazon S3 bucket, or an Amazon EFS file system. For more information, see Storage options for your Amazon EC2 instances.

###### Amazon EBS volumes

When an instance is terminated, the EBS volumes are either deleted or preserved, depending on the value of the `DeleteOnTermination` attribute for each volume:

  * Yes (console) / `true` (CLI) – The volume is deleted when the instance is terminated.

  * No (console) / `false` (CLI) – The volume is preserved when the instance is terminated. Preserved volumes continue to incur charges.

###### Note

After an instance terminates, you can take a snapshot of the preserved volume or attach it to another instance. To avoid incurring charges, you must delete the volume.

## Default deletion behavior for EBS volumes

The default `DeleteOnTermination` value differs depending on the volume type, whether the volume was attached at launch or after, and the method (console or CLI) used to attach the volume:

Volume type  | Attached when  | Method for attaching  | Default behavior on instance termination
--- | --- | --- | ---
Root volume  | At launch  | Console or CLI  | Delete
Root volume  | After launch  | Console or CLI  | Preserve
Data volume  | At launch  | Console  | Preserve
Data volume  | At launch  | CLI  | Delete
Data volume  | After launch  | Console and CLI  | Preserve

## Check volume persistence settings

The default value at launch for an EBS volume is determined by the `DeleteOnTermination` attribute set on the AMI. You can change the value at instance launch, overriding the AMI setting. We recommend that you verify the default setting for the `DeleteOnTermination` attribute after you launch an instance.

###### To check if an Amazon EBS volume will be deleted on instance termination

  1. Open the Amazon EC2 console at https://console.aws.amazon.com/ec2/.

  2. In the navigation pane, choose Instances.

  3. Select the instance.

  4. Choose the Storage tab.

  5. Under Block devices, scroll right to check the Delete on termination column.

     * If Yes, the volume is deleted when the instance is terminated.

     * If No, the volume is not be deleted when the instance is terminated. Any volumes not deleted continue to incur charges.

## Change the root volume to persist at launch

You can change the `DeleteOnTermination` attribute of an EBS root volume when you launch an instance. You can also use the following procedure for a data volume.

If you enable termination protection, you can't terminate the instance using the console, CLI, or API.

After you terminate an instance, it remains visible in the console for a short while, and then the entry is automatically deleted. You can also describe a terminated instance using the CLI and API. Resources (such as tags) are gradually disassociated from the terminated instance, therefore may no longer be visible on the terminated instance after a short while. You can't connect to or recover a terminated instance.

Each Amazon EBS-backed instance supports the `InstanceInitiatedShutdownBehavior` attribute, which controls whether the instance stops or terminates when you initiate shutdown from within the instance itself (for example, by using the shutdown command on Linux). The default behavior is to stop the instance. You can modify the setting of this attribute while the instance is running or stopped.

Each Amazon EBS volume supports the `DeleteOnTermination` attribute, which controls whether the volume is deleted or preserved when you terminate the instance it is attached to. The default is to delete the root volume and preserve any other EBS volumes.

For more information, see Terminate Amazon EC2 instances.

In this task, you'll stop your instance to preserve your Free Tier benefits. When your instance is stopped, you stop incurring costs for it. If you created your AWS account before July 15, 2025 and you qualify for the Free Tier, you will continue to incur costs for the EBS storage.

  1. Initiate stopping:

If you're still on the Connect to instance page, choose Instances from the breadcrumb. If you've navigated away, choose Instances from the navigation pane.

Then, on the Instances page, select the checkbox next to the name of your instance, and then choose the Instance state menu (top right), and choose Stop instance. When prompted, choose Stop.

On the Instances page, check the Instance state column. The state of your instance changes to Stopping and then Stopped. If you don't see the full text, try widening the column.

# QuickHealth on one AWS EC2 server

This guide prepares one Ubuntu server in **US East (N. Virginia), `us-east-1`** and makes QuickHealth reachable from the public internet, including Nigeria. It uses the AWS web console and the browser-based EC2 Instance Connect option. It does not use AWS CLI.

## Before you launch

- Use fictional cases only. QuickHealth is a hackathon prototype, not medical advice, and has not been clinically validated. Do not enter real patient information.
- This prototype saves conversations in a SQLite database on the server. Its saved-session screen is not private between visitors. Do not share this public URL for sensitive use; a visitor may be able to see saved fictional sessions from other visitors.
- Check your hackathon credits or allowance in the AWS Billing console before launching. Choose one small x86-64 instance that the console shows is covered. A `t3.small` (2 GiB RAM) is a practical starting point if your allowance covers it. The smallest `t3.micro` may run out of memory while installing dependencies or serving the app.
- The app is served over HTTP on port 8501, without TLS or a domain name. Anyone who knows the public address can reach it. This guide does not add a login or geographic restriction.
- No AWS cost can be guaranteed here. Check the billing and credits pages, and terminate the instance and remove leftover billable resources when finished.

## 1. Choose the AWS Region

1. Sign in to the AWS web console.
2. Use the Region menu in the upper right and choose **US East (N. Virginia) (`us-east-1`)**.

## 2. Create a security group

The instance needs two inbound rules: port 22 for the AWS browser connection and port 8501 for visitors using the app. Do not create a port 22 rule open to `0.0.0.0/0`.

1. Open **EC2** from the AWS console search bar.
2. In the left menu, choose **Network & Security â†’ Security Groups**, then **Create security group**.
3. Name it `quickhealth-web` and choose the default VPC.
4. Under **Inbound rules**, add:
   - **SSH**, port **22**, source **Custom**: select the prefix list `com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ec2-instance-connect`.
   - **Custom TCP**, port **8501**, source **Anywhere-IPv4** (`0.0.0.0/0`). This is the public app port; it permits connections from Nigeria and other locations without a country filter.
5. Keep the default outbound rule allowing traffic out. The server needs outbound internet access to install packages and contact OpenAI and Neatlogs.
6. Choose **Create security group**.

AWS documents the Instance Connect prefix-list rule in its [browser connection setup guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-instance-connect-tutorial.html).

## 3. Launch one Ubuntu instance

1. In EC2, choose **Instances â†’ Launch instances**.
2. Enter `quickhealth-demo` as the name.
3. Under **Application and OS Images**, choose **Ubuntu**, then an Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS x86-64 image.
4. Under **Instance type**, select one small size that is covered by your hackathon allowance. Use `t3.small` if covered; otherwise check with the hackathon organizer before choosing a larger type.
5. Under **Key pair (login)**, choose **Proceed without a key pair**. The browser-based EC2 Instance Connect flow supplies its temporary connection key.
6. Under **Network settings**, choose the default VPC and a subnet that assigns a public IPv4 address. Enable **Auto-assign public IP**.
7. Choose **Select existing security group** and select `quickhealth-web`.
8. Under **Configure storage**, keep one modest root volume (for example, 12 GiB) and make sure **Delete on termination** is enabled for it.
9. Check the Summary for one instance, the `us-east-1` Region, and the covered instance type. Choose **Launch instance**.

## 4. Connect in the browser

1. In **EC2 â†’ Instances**, wait for `quickhealth-demo` to show **Running** and pass its status checks.
2. Select it and choose **Connect**.
3. Choose **EC2 Instance Connect**, keep the browser connection option, and choose **Connect**.
4. A browser terminal opens. The commands in the next steps are Linux commands for this server, not AWS commands.

If the browser connection fails, check that inbound port 22 is restricted to the `us-east-1` Instance Connect prefix list and that the instance has a public IPv4 address.

## 5. Download and run the installer

In the browser terminal, download the setup script from this public repository, inspect it, then run it as an administrator. This script installs Python and Git, clones the public repository, installs its Python requirements in a virtual environment, creates the environment-file template, and installs and starts a systemd service.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dynaayowilliams-dot/quickhealth/main/deploy/aws/setup.sh -o /tmp/quickhealth-setup.sh
less /tmp/quickhealth-setup.sh
sudo bash /tmp/quickhealth-setup.sh
```

The app files are installed in `/opt/quickhealth`. The service starts, but model-backed features will not work until you enter the required values on the server in the next step.

## 6. Enter secrets directly on the server

The checked-in template at `deploy/aws/quickhealth.env.template` lists variable names only. The installer copies it to `/opt/quickhealth/.env` and restricts that file to the `quickhealth` service account. The repository's `.gitignore` excludes `.env`.

1. In the browser terminal, open the server-only file with `sudo nano /opt/quickhealth/.env`.
2. On the server, fill in the values for `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_MODEL`, and `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`. Type or paste them directly into this editor. Do not put real values in GitHub, this repository, this README, or a command line.
3. Save in nano with **Ctrl+O**, press **Enter**, then exit with **Ctrl+X**.
4. Restart the app service:

   ```bash
   sudo systemctl restart quickhealth
   ```

Never send the key values to anyone or include them in screenshots or support messages. To change a value later, edit this server-only file and restart the service.

## 7. Open the app

1. In the AWS console, open **EC2 â†’ Instances**, select `quickhealth-demo`, and copy its **Public IPv4 address**.
2. In a browser, open `http://PUBLIC-IP:8501`, replacing `PUBLIC-IP` with the copied address.
3. Confirm the QuickHealth banner still says fictional cases only and that it is not medical advice. Do not enter real health information.

The public IPv4 address may change after a stop and start. This setup does not reserve a paid static address.

## If the app does not start

In the browser terminal, inspect service status and recent service logs:

```bash
sudo systemctl status quickhealth --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u quickhealth -n 60 --no-pager
```

The service restarts automatically after a failure. Check that the environment file has all three values, then restart the service. Never paste secret values into logs or support requests.

## Shut everything down when finished

Stopping an instance leaves its disk behind and can continue storage charges. To end this demo and avoid leaving the server online:

1. In the AWS console, open **EC2 â†’ Instances**, select `quickhealth-demo`, then choose **Instance state â†’ Terminate (delete) instance** and confirm.
2. Wait until the instance shows **Terminated**.
3. In **EC2 â†’ Volumes**, check that the root volume was deleted. Delete any unattached volume created for this demo if you no longer need it.
4. In **EC2 â†’ Elastic IPs**, confirm you did not allocate an unused address; release one if you created it and no longer need it.
5. In **EC2 â†’ Security Groups**, delete `quickhealth-web` after no instance uses it.
6. Check **Billing â†’ Bills** and **Credits** for any remaining resources or charges.

Terminating the instance deletes its local SQLite database if the root volume is deleted. AWS explains that preserved EBS volumes continue to incur storage charges in its [volume termination guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/preserving-volumes-on-termination.html).

# QuickHealth on one AWS EC2 server

This guide prepares one Ubuntu server in **US East (N. Virginia), `us-east-1`** and makes QuickHealth reachable from the public internet, including Nigeria. It uses the AWS web console and the browser-based EC2 Instance Connect option. It does not use AWS CLI.

## Before you launch

- Use fictional cases only. QuickHealth is a hackathon prototype, not medical advice, and has not been clinically validated. Do not enter real patient information.
- This prototype saves conversations in a SQLite database on the server. Its saved-session screen is not private between visitors. Do not share this public URL for sensitive use; a visitor may be able to see saved fictional sessions from other visitors.
- Check your hackathon credits or allowance in the AWS Billing console before launching. Choose one small x86-64 instance that the console shows is covered. A `t3.small` (2 GiB RAM) is a practical starting point if your allowance covers it. The smallest `t3.micro` may run out of memory while installing dependencies or serving the app.
- The app is served over HTTP on port 8501, without TLS or a domain name. Anyone who knows the public address can reach it. This guide does not add a login or geographic restriction.
- No AWS cost can be guaranteed here. Check the billing and credits pages, and terminate the instance and remove leftover billable resources when finished.

## 1. Choose the AWS Region

1. Sign in to the AWS web console.
2. Use the Region menu in the upper right and choose **US East (N. Virginia) (`us-east-1`)**.

## 2. Create a security group

The instance needs two inbound rules: port 22 for the AWS browser connection and port 8501 for visitors using the app. Do not create a port 22 rule open to `0.0.0.0/0`.

1. Open **EC2** from the AWS console search bar.
2. In the left menu, choose **Network & Security â†’ Security Groups**, then **Create security group**.
3. Name it `quickhealth-web` and choose the default VPC.
4. Under **Inbound rules**, add:
   - **SSH**, port **22**, source **Custom**: select the prefix list `com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ec2-instance-connect`.
   - **Custom TCP**, port **8501**, source **Anywhere-IPv4** (`0.0.0.0/0`). This is the public app port; it permits connections from Nigeria and other locations without a country filter.
5. Keep the default outbound rule allowing traffic out. The server needs outbound internet access to install packages and contact OpenAI and Neatlogs.
6. Choose **Create security group**.

AWS documents the Instance Connect prefix-list rule in its [browser connection setup guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-instance-connect-tutorial.html).

## 3. Launch one Ubuntu instance

1. In EC2, choose **Instances â†’ Launch instances**.
2. Enter `quickhealth-demo` as the name.
3. Under **Application and OS Images**, choose **Ubuntu**, then an Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS x86-64 image.
4. Under **Instance type**, select one small size that is covered by your hackathon allowance. Use `t3.small` if covered; otherwise check with the hackathon organizer before choosing a larger type.
5. Under **Key pair (login)**, choose **Proceed without a key pair**. The browser-based EC2 Instance Connect flow supplies its temporary connection key.
6. Under **Network settings**, choose the default VPC and a subnet that assigns a public IPv4 address. Enable **Auto-assign public IP**.
7. Choose **Select existing security group** and select `quickhealth-web`.
8. Under **Configure storage**, keep one modest root volume (for example, 12 GiB) and make sure **Delete on termination** is enabled for it.
9. Check the Summary for one instance, the `us-east-1` Region, and the covered instance type. Choose **Launch instance**.

## 4. Connect in the browser

1. In **EC2 â†’ Instances**, wait for `quickhealth-demo` to show **Running** and pass its status checks.
2. Select it and choose **Connect**.
3. Choose **EC2 Instance Connect**, keep the browser connection option, and choose **Connect**.
4. A browser terminal opens. The commands in the next steps are Linux commands for this server, not AWS commands.

If the browser connection fails, check that inbound port 22 is restricted to the `us-east-1` Instance Connect prefix list and that the instance has a public IPv4 address.

## 5. Download and run the installer

In the browser terminal, download the setup script from this public repository, inspect it, then run it as an administrator. This script installs Python and Git, clones the public repository, installs its Python requirements in a virtual environment, creates the environment-file template, and installs and starts a systemd service.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dynaayowilliams-dot/quickhealth/main/deploy/aws/setup.sh -o /tmp/quickhealth-setup.sh
less /tmp/quickhealth-setup.sh
sudo bash /tmp/quickhealth-setup.sh
```

The app files are installed in `/opt/quickhealth`. The service starts, but model-backed features will not work until you enter the required values on the server in the next step.

## 6. Enter secrets directly on the server

The checked-in template at `deploy/aws/quickhealth.env.template` lists variable names only. The installer copies it to `/opt/quickhealth/.env` and restricts that file to the `quickhealth` service account. The repository's `.gitignore` excludes `.env`.

1. In the browser terminal, open the server-only file with `sudo nano /opt/quickhealth/.env`.
2. On the server, fill in the values for `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_MODEL`, and `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`. Type or paste them directly into this editor. Do not put real values in GitHub, this repository, this README, or a command line.
3. Save in nano with **Ctrl+O**, press **Enter**, then exit with **Ctrl+X**.
4. Restart the app service:

   ```bash
   sudo systemctl restart quickhealth
   ```

Never send the key values to anyone or include them in screenshots or support messages. To change a value later, edit this server-only file and restart the service.

## 7. Open the app

1. In the AWS console, open **EC2 â†’ Instances**, select `quickhealth-demo`, and copy its **Public IPv4 address**.
2. In a browser, open `http://PUBLIC-IP:8501`, replacing `PUBLIC-IP` with the copied address.
3. Confirm the QuickHealth banner still says fictional cases only and that it is not medical advice. Do not enter real health information.

The public IPv4 address may change after a stop and start. This setup does not reserve a paid static address.

## If the app does not start

In the browser terminal, inspect service status and recent service logs:

```bash
sudo systemctl status quickhealth --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u quickhealth -n 60 --no-pager
```

The service restarts automatically after a failure. Check that the environment file has all three values, then restart the service. Never paste secret values into logs or support requests.

## Shut everything down when finished

Stopping an instance leaves its disk behind and can continue storage charges. To end this demo and avoid leaving the server online:

1. In the AWS console, open **EC2 â†’ Instances**, select `quickhealth-demo`, then choose **Instance state â†’ Terminate (delete) instance** and confirm.
2. Wait until the instance shows **Terminated**.
3. In **EC2 â†’ Volumes**, check that the root volume was deleted. Delete any unattached volume created for this demo if you no longer need it.
4. In **EC2 â†’ Elastic IPs**, confirm you did not allocate an unused address; release one if you created it and no longer need it.
5. In **EC2 â†’ Security Groups**, delete `quickhealth-web` after no instance uses it.
6. Check **Billing â†’ Bills** and **Credits** for any remaining resources or charges.

Terminating the instance deletes its local SQLite database if the root volume is deleted. AWS explains that preserved EBS volumes continue to incur storage charges in its [volume termination guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/preserving-volumes-on-termination.html).

## Before you launch

- Use fictional cases only. QuickHealth is a hackathon prototype, not medical advice, and has not been clinically validated. Do not enter real patient information.
- This prototype saves conversations in a SQLite database on the server. Its saved-session screen is not private between visitors. Do not share this public URL for sensitive use; a visitor may be able to see saved fictional sessions from other visitors.
- Check your hackathon credits or allowance in the AWS Billing console before launching. Choose one small x86-64 instance that the console shows is covered. A `t3.small` (2 GiB RAM) is a practical starting point if your allowance covers it. The smallest `t3.micro` may run out of memory while installing dependencies or serving the app.
- The app is served over HTTP on port 8501, without TLS or a domain name. Anyone who knows the public address can reach it. This guide does not add a login or geographic restriction.
- No AWS cost can be guaranteed here. Check the billing and credits pages, and terminate the instance and remove leftover billable resources when finished.

## 1. Choose the AWS Region

1. Sign in to the AWS web console.
2. Use the Region menu in the upper right and choose **US East (N. Virginia) (`us-east-1`)**.

## 2. Create a security group

The instance needs two inbound rules: port 22 for the AWS browser connection and port 8501 for visitors using the app. Do not create a port 22 rule open to `0.0.0.0/0`.

1. Open **EC2** from the AWS console search bar.
2. In the left menu, choose **Network & Security â†’ Security Groups**, then **Create security group**.
3. Name it `quickhealth-web` and choose the default VPC.
4. Under **Inbound rules**, add:
   - **SSH**, port **22**, source **Custom**: select the prefix list `com.amazonaws.us-east-1.ec2-instance-connect`.
   - **Custom TCP**, port **8501**, source **Anywhere-IPv4** (`0.0.0.0/0`). This is the public app port; it permits connections from Nigeria and other locations without a country filter.
5. Keep the default outbound rule allowing traffic out. The server needs outbound internet access to install packages and contact OpenAI and Neatlogs.
6. Choose **Create security group**.

AWS documents the Instance Connect prefix-list rule in its [browser connection setup guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-instance-connect-tutorial.html).

## 3. Launch one Ubuntu instance

1. In EC2, choose **Instances â†’ Launch instances**.
2. Enter `quickhealth-demo` as the name.
3. Under **Application and OS Images**, choose **Ubuntu**, then an Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS x86-64 image.
4. Under **Instance type**, select one small size that is covered by your hackathon allowance. Use `t3.small` if covered; otherwise check with the hackathon organizer before choosing a larger type.
5. Under **Key pair (login)**, choose **Proceed without a key pair**. The browser-based EC2 Instance Connect flow supplies its temporary connection key.
6. Under **Network settings**, choose the default VPC and a subnet that assigns a public IPv4 address. Enable **Auto-assign public IP**.
7. Choose **Select existing security group** and select `quickhealth-web`.
8. Under **Configure storage**, keep one modest root volume (for example, 12 GiB) and make sure **Delete on termination** is enabled for it.
9. Check the Summary for one instance, the `us-east-1` Region, and the covered instance type. Choose **Launch instance**.

## 4. Connect in the browser

1. In **EC2 â†’ Instances**, wait for `quickhealth-demo` to show **Running** and pass its status checks.
2. Select it and choose **Connect**.
3. Choose **EC2 Instance Connect**, keep the browser connection option, and choose **Connect**.
4. A browser terminal opens. The commands in the next steps are Linux commands for this server, not AWS commands.

If the browser connection fails, check that inbound port 22 is restricted to the `us-east-1` Instance Connect prefix list and that the instance has a public IPv4 address.

## 5. Download and run the installer

In the browser terminal, download the setup script from this public repository, inspect it, then run it as an administrator. This script installs Python and Git, clones the public repository, installs its Python requirements in a virtual environment, creates the environment-file template, and installs and starts a systemd service.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dynaayowilliams-dot/quickhealth/main/deploy/aws/setup.sh -o /tmp/quickhealth-setup.sh
less /tmp/quickhealth-setup.sh
sudo bash /tmp/quickhealth-setup.sh
```

The app files are installed in `/opt/quickhealth`. The service starts, but model-backed features will not work until you enter the required values on the server in the next step.

## 6. Enter secrets directly on the server

The checked-in template at `deploy/aws/quickhealth.env.template` lists variable names only. The installer copies it to `/opt/quickhealth/.env` and restricts that file to the `quickhealth` service account. The repository's `.gitignore` excludes `.env`.

1. In the browser terminal, open the server-only file with `sudo nano /opt/quickhealth/.env`.
2. On the server, fill in the values for `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_MODEL`, and `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`. Type or paste them directly into this editor. Do not put real values in GitHub, this repository, this README, or a command line.
3. Save in nano with **Ctrl+O**, press **Enter**, then exit with **Ctrl+X**.
4. Restart the app service:

   ```bash
   sudo systemctl restart quickhealth
   ```

Never send the key values to anyone or include them in screenshots or support messages. To change a value later, edit this server-only file and restart the service.

## 7. Open the app

1. In the AWS console, open **EC2 â†’ Instances**, select `quickhealth-demo`, and copy its **Public IPv4 address**.
2. In a browser, open `http://PUBLIC-IP:8501`, replacing `PUBLIC-IP` with the copied address.
3. Confirm the QuickHealth banner still says fictional cases only and that it is not medical advice. Do not enter real health information.

The public IPv4 address may change after a stop and start. This setup does not reserve a paid static address.

## If the app does not start

In the browser terminal, inspect service status and recent service logs:

```bash
sudo systemctl status quickhealth --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u quickhealth -n 60 --no-pager
```

The service restarts automatically after a failure. Check that the environment file has all three values, then restart the service. Never paste secret values into logs or support requests.

## Shut everything down when finished

Stopping an instance leaves its disk behind and can continue storage charges. To end this demo and avoid leaving the server online:

1. In the AWS console, open **EC2 â†’ Instances**, select `quickhealth-demo`, then choose **Instance state â†’ Terminate (delete) instance** and confirm.
2. Wait until the instance shows **Terminated**.
3. In **EC2 â†’ Volumes**, check that the root volume was deleted. Delete any unattached volume created for this demo if you no longer need it.
4. In **EC2 â†’ Elastic IPs**, confirm you did not allocate an unused address; release one if you created it and no longer need it.
5. In **EC2 â†’ Security Groups**, delete `quickhealth-web` after no instance uses it.
6. Check **Billing â†’ Bills** and **Credits** for any remaining resources or charges.

Terminating the instance deletes its local SQLite database if the root volume is deleted. AWS explains that preserved EBS volumes continue to incur storage charges in its [volume termination guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/preserving-volumes-on-termination.html).

import json
